system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: IgG1/IgG3 autoantibodies against postsynaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptors can functionally block receptors, accelerate receptor internalization, and activate complement, reducing functional receptor density and damaging the postsynaptic membrane.
vignette: A young adult has fluctuating ptosis, diplopia, and fatigable bulbar weakness that worsens late in the day. Sensation and reflexes are normal. Serum testing detects antibodies against the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor.
lead: Which pathophysiologic process most directly reduces neuromuscular transmission in this patient?
correct: Autoantibody-mediated loss and complement injury of postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors
distractors: Autoantibody-mediated blockade of presynaptic P/Q-type calcium channels
Failure of synaptic-vesicle acetylcholine release caused by botulinum neurotoxin
Degeneration of anterior-horn motor neurons with denervation
Defective dystrophin anchoring of the muscle-cell cytoskeleton
distractor_notes: Presynaptic P/Q-type calcium-channel antibodies cause Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome, which typically features autonomic symptoms, hyporeflexia, and facilitation.
Botulism is a toxin-mediated presynaptic release defect with an acute clinical context.
Anterior-horn-cell degeneration causes motor-neuron disease, not a postsynaptic autoantibody disorder.
Dystrophin defects cause muscular dystrophy rather than fatigable autoimmune neuromuscular-junction weakness.
key_expl: In AChR-positive myasthenia gravis, pathogenic IgG binds the postsynaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptor. Antibodies can block receptor function, increase receptor endocytosis, and activate complement, damaging the postsynaptic membrane and reducing the safety factor for neuromuscular transmission.
objective: Explain AChR-positive myasthenia gravis as antibody-mediated postsynaptic receptor loss and complement injury.
